newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Caribbean nations stand up to U.S. over drugs.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean nations stand up to U.S. over drugs.

text.p: Caribbean leaders, stung by U.S. accusations that they are dragging their feet in the war against drugs, vowed they would not bow to threats and coercion by Washington.

Eight government heads meeting in Bridgetown on Monday on the dispute with the United States over drugs policy said the fight against narcotics was critically important but should be based on co-operation and mutually acceptable treaties.
They rejected "any suggestion or threat of coercive measures as a means of extracting compliance with predetermined policies."

"Unfounded allegations, innuendoes and the threat of punitive measures aimed at the economic welfare of Caribbean states would only weaken the collective effort against drug trafficking and undermine the foundations of the good relations which the region has enjoyed and seeks to maintain with the United States," a communique said.

U.S. officials believe a third of the cocaine and heroin reaching the United States from Latin America comes through the Caribbean. Washington demands tougher action from the small Caribbean nations and wants them to agree to treaties on extradition and patrolling their waters.

But they fear their sovereignty is threatened. The Jamaican government was enraged this month when Patricia Hall, a U.S. State Department official, said it had failed to pursue suspects, including at least one elected official.

The summit said the drugs issue must be seen as part of wider social and economic problems in the Caribbean. The leaders want to meet President Bill Clinton early next year to discuss trade and economic development as well as the anti-narcotics effort.
